_meta.scope: Application-side demand cases priced from structured US federal award data (USAspending.gov API, EPA Clean Ports, DoD ESPC/UESC/utility-privatization vehicles) rather than press releases, so every record carries an obligated or total-potential contract value tied to a named site.
angles_run: USAspending /api/v2/search/spending_by_award keyword sweeps: microgrid, diesel generator, standby generator, shore power, cold ironing, energy savings performance contract, utility privatization, Clean Ports, port electrification, Grid Resilience
USAspending /api/v2/awards/{id} detail pulls to separate total_obligation from base_and_all_options on multi-decade vehicles
EPA Clean Ports Program (CFDA 66.051) award records for per-port federal + cost-share values and equipment counts
Confirmation of two named leads: Parris Island ESPC and NAVFAC Beaufort utility privatization
Capacity (MW) corroboration from contractor and Navy publications where the award record gives dollars but not megawatts
absences: USAspending keyword 'cold ironing' returned zero awards in FY2008-FY2026 — the term does not appear in federal contract descriptions, so shore power is the only searchable handle.

DOT/MARAD Port Infrastructure Development Program: not resolved to per-award records inside this pass; PIDP awards are announced by press release and did not surface under the keyword sweeps used here.

FEMA BRIC and Hazard Mitigation Grant Program generator/microgrid awards: not retrieved. OpenFEMA datasets were not queried in this pass, so no named-site FEMA generator dollar values are in this file.
DOE Energy Improvements in Rural or Remote Areas (ERA): USAspending keyword 'Energy Improvements in Rural or Remote Areas' returned zero grant awards, so ERA site-level values are absent.

Off-grid mining & mineral processing: no federal award record with a named mine site and a generation dollar value was found; DOE MESC critical-minerals awards fund processing plants, not the power blocks, so nothing in that sector is recorded here.

No award record published a $/kWh energy price. Federal construction and ESPC awards publish capital and lifecycle dollars, not tariffs, so every price figure here is capex or contract value, never an energy rate.
Heat rate, fuel burn and annual generation are not in the award records; where a $/MWh comparison would be useful it could not be derived from the award's own numbers.

cases.name: Fort Stewart 10 MW generation plant with microgrid controls (W912HN26CA001)
cases.capacity: 10 MW generation plant with microgrid controls
cases.capex: $54,333,598 obligated; base and all options also $54,333,598 (firm, no unexercised options)
cases.displaced: Grid dependence at an Army installation; the award buys islandable on-site generation rather than replacing an existing plant
cases.summary: USACE Savannah District awarded David Boland Inc. a definitive construction contract on 2025-11-03 to build a 10 MW generation plant with microgrid controls at Fort Stewart, Georgia, with a period of performance running to 2028-12-15. The award record shows $54,333,598 obligated and an identical base-and-all-options value, so this is the whole contract, not a first tranche. Place of performance is recorded as FORT STEWART, LIBERTY COUNTY, GA 31315. The award is a construction contract only — no fuel, no operations, no long-term service.
cases.microreactor_read: This is the cleanest federal price stamp available for on-site firm generation at a defended site: $54.33M for 10 MW is $5,433/kW of installed capacity, engineering and construction included, with fuel and O&M still to come on top. A 1-20 MW microreactor sold into an Army installation has to land near or below $5,400/kW installed to be argued on capital cost alone, and its pitch has to be the fuel and O&M line the Boland contract does not cover.

cases.name: MCRD Parris Island site-wide microgrid ESPC (N39430-17-F-1901)
cases.capacity: 3.5 MW natural-gas CHP + 6.7 MW-DC solar PV + 8.0 MWh battery + existing diesel backup, under one microgrid controller; announced as 10 MW of new on-site generation
cases.price: $91.1 million self-funding ESPC investment as announced by the contractor
cases.capex: $66,631,952 obligated to date against a base-and-all-options value of $212,716,674 (USAspending, award last modified 2026-05-01)
cases.displaced: An end-of-life central steam plant and grid purchases; announced as a 79% reduction in the depot's utility energy demand

filings.type: ESPC task order under DOE IDIQ DE-AM36-09GO29029

cases.summary: NAVFAC EXWC issued Ameresco a task order under the DOE ESPC IDIQ on 2016-12-28 to build and then operate a site-wide microgrid at Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island, with a period of performance running to 2041-11-30. Ameresco announced the deal as a $91.1 million self-funding ESPC covering 10 MW of new on-site generation, a 3.5 MW gas CHP plant replacing the end-of-life steam plant, 6.7 MW-DC of solar PV and an 8.0 MWh battery. The federal award record tells a different story about size: $66,631,952 has been obligated so far and the contract's base-and-all-options value is $212,716,674 — 2.3x the announced $91.1M, because the ESPC's later years are performance-period service payments, not construction. The host pays nothing up front and repays out of guaranteed savings across roughly 25 years.
cases.microreactor_read: Two numbers matter to a microreactor seller here and they are far apart: the capital comparison is $91.1M for about 10 MW of mixed generation, i.e. roughly $9,100/kW nameplate and about $26,000/kW if you count only the 3.5 MW of firm dispatchable CHP; the commercial comparison is the $212.7M of lifecycle contract value a 25-year vehicle at one recruit depot can actually carry. A 5-10 MW microreactor priced against the $91.1M sticker looks expensive and priced against the $212.7M lifecycle envelope looks financeable — which is why the instrument, not the capex, is the thing to copy.

cases.name: Naval Station Guantanamo Bay 20 MW LNG combined-cycle plant ESPC (N39430-19-F-9909)
cases.capacity: 20 MW LNG dual-fuel combined-cycle plant, plus a 13.7 MW solar facility; 15 existing diesel generators retained for outages and peaks
cases.price: Projected annual energy savings of $24.6 million over a 22-year performance period
cases.capex: $368.8 million for the power plant itself; $828.8 million announced ESPC value; USAspending shows $101,059,504 obligated against a base-and-all-options value of $927,391,394 running to 2043-04-24
cases.displaced: Diesel generation on an isolated island base — LNG substitution announced at approximately $9 million a year in fuel cost savings versus diesel, and a 27.4 percent cut in annual fuel consumption

filings.type: ESPC task order under DOE IDIQ DE-AM36-09GO29041, firm fixed price

cases.summary: In July 2019 NAVFAC Southeast awarded Siemens Government Technologies an ESPC task order — announced at $828.8 million and issued for 25 years of construction plus operation — to replace diesel generation at Naval Station Guantanamo Bay with a dual-fuel LNG combined-cycle plant and a solar field. The plant was commissioned on 2023-09-07 and is rated 20 MW; the plant alone cost $368.8 million. The federal award record shows $101,059,504 obligated so far against a base-and-all-options value of $927,391,394 with a potential end date of 2043-04-24, so the contract has grown roughly $100M past its announced value and only about 11 percent of the ceiling has been obligated. The 15 pre-existing diesel generators were not retired; they were kept for outages and peaks.
cases.microreactor_read: Guantanamo is the strongest capex-per-MW argument in this file and it runs the reactor's way: $368.8M for 20 MW of island generation is $18,440/kW, and that is for a gas plant whose fuel still has to arrive by ship. A 1-20 MW microreactor competing at an isolated base does not need to beat $5,400/kW — at a site with no pipeline and no grid tie it needs to beat roughly $18,000/kW plus a fuel logistics chain, against a counterfactual the Navy itself valued at $24.6M a year in savings over 22 years.

cases.name: Doyon Utilities 50-year utility privatization, Alaska Army installations (SP0600-07-C-8263)
cases.region: Fort Wainwright, Alaska (plus Fort Greely and JBER-Richardson under the Doyon Utilities program)

parties.host: U.S. Army, contracting through DLA Energy
parties.provider: Doyon Utilities, LLC (Alaska Native corporation joint venture)
parties.utility: Doyon Utilities, LLC — regulated by the Regulatory Commission of Alaska

cases.capacity: Full electric, heat, water and wastewater utility systems at Alaska Army installations; capacity not stated in the award record
cases.capex: $894,733,810 obligated to date against a base-and-all-options value of $3,082,072,958; period of performance 2007-09-28 to 2058-08-14
cases.displaced: Government ownership and operation of installation utility systems in interior Alaska, where the incumbent generation is coal and oil-fired central plant

filings.type: Utility service contract for utility privatization, firm fixed price
Companion utility privatization contract, same recipient and date

cases.summary: DLA Energy awarded Doyon Utilities a utility privatization contract on 2007-09-28 covering Army installation utility systems in Alaska, with a period of performance that runs to 2058-08-14 — a fifty-one year term. The award record shows $894,733,810 already obligated and a base-and-all-options value of $3,082,072,958, making this by a wide margin the largest single utility vehicle surfaced in this sweep. A companion contract to the same recipient on the same day (SP0600-07-C-8261) carries a further $212,665,748 obligated. The contractor is a regulated utility: its rates at these installations are set by the Regulatory Commission of Alaska, not by the contract alone.
cases.microreactor_read: This is the instrument a microreactor should be sold into rather than around: a single counterparty already holds a fifty-year, three-billion-dollar franchise to supply heat and power to Alaska Army installations, and its generation is coal and oil in a place where fuel arrives by rail and barge. The reactor does not need to beat a $/kW number to enter — it needs to become an asset inside a rate base a regulator already approves, and the addressable line is the roughly $60M a year of obligations this one contract has averaged since 2007.

cases.name: Port of Los Angeles zero-emission technology deployment, EPA Clean Ports Program (97T27601)

parties.host: City of Los Angeles Harbor Department (Port of Los Angeles), with subawards to terminals YTI, APMT, Everport, Fenix and TraPac
parties.utility: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power

cases.capacity: 337 battery-electric yard tractors, 250 zero-emission trucks, 56 battery-electric top handlers, 32 battery-electric heavy lifts, a vessel shore power system, roughly 143 MWh of battery capacity, 307 chargers and 10 battery-solar systems
cases.capex: $411,688,296 federal obligation plus $232,523,864 non-federal cost share, $644,212,160 total funding; period of performance 2025-01-01 to 2028-12-31
cases.displaced: Diesel cargo-handling equipment and drayage trucks, and at-berth vessel auxiliary diesel via the new shore power system

filings.type: Grant under CFDA 66.051, Clean Ports Program (Inflation Reduction Act)

cases.summary: EPA obligated $411,688,296 to the City of Los Angeles Harbor Department under the Inflation Reduction Act's Clean Ports Program, with $232,523,864 in non-federal cost share for a total project value of $644,212,160 running 2025-01-01 to 2028-12-31. The scope is not a power plant — it is the load: 337 battery-electric yard tractors, 250 zero-emission trucks, 56 top handlers, 32 heavy lifts, a vessel shore power system, about 143 MWh of on-site battery capacity, 307 chargers and 10 battery-solar systems, spread across five container terminals as subawards. This is a single-port grant that creates a large new around-the-clock electrical demand at one place on the coast, funded up front by a grant rather than by a supply contract.
cases.microreactor_read: The Clean Ports award buys the demand and leaves the supply unsolved: 143 MWh of batteries and 307 chargers at one port is a multi-tens-of-MW peak that has to come from LADWP's distribution system on a schedule set by ship calls, not by the grid. A microreactor seller's opening here is not a $/kW comparison against the $644M of equipment — it is the interconnection upgrade the port has not funded, and the reactor has to be cheaper than the terminal's alternative of paying for a distribution upgrade plus demand charges on a load that is 100 percent electrified by 2030 mandate.

cases.name: Naval Base Ventura County / Point Mugu shore power mound repair and replacement (N62473-24-F-4934)
cases.capacity: Shore power mounds serving berthed vessels; megawatt rating not stated in the award record
cases.capex: $44,323,562 obligated; base and all options identical, so the full contract value is $44.3M with no unexercised options
cases.displaced: Vessel auxiliary diesel generation at berth, and end-of-life shore power distribution equipment

filings.type: Design-build task order under IDIQ N6247324D5205

cases.summary: NAVFAC Southwest awarded South Bay EDC a design-build task order on 2024-07-28 to repair and replace the shore power mound at Naval Base Ventura County / Point Mugu, California, with a period of performance to 2027-05-27. The obligated value and the base-and-all-options value are both $44,323,562, so this is the whole job. The award funds only the pierside electrical connection — the distribution equipment that lets a berthed vessel shut down its own diesels — and buys no generation whatsoever.
cases.microreactor_read: Shore power at one naval berthing complex costs $44.3M in electrical infrastructure alone, before a single megawatt-hour is generated, and the Navy pays it to move vessel load onto the shore grid. That number is the honest floor a microreactor has to sit under to be worth siting at a marine terminal: if a 5 MW unit plus its own switchgear lands anywhere near $44M, it competes directly with the connection cost the Navy is already paying, and it also removes the shore-grid capacity constraint the mound alone does not solve.

parties.host: U.S. Navy / NAVFAC (MCRD Parris Island, MCAS Beaufort, Naval Hospital Beaufort, Laurel Bay housing)

cases.capacity: Water distribution and wastewater collection systems at four Navy and Marine Corps sites; no electric generation in scope
cases.capex: $20,987,602.80 obligated as of the record's last modification on 2019-07-16, against a base-and-all-options value of $254,977,740.80; period of performance 2008-02-28 to 2058-02-27
cases.displaced: Government ownership and operation of the installations' water and wastewater systems

filings.type: Utility privatization contract, fixed price redetermination

cases.summary: This record exists to correct a lead. The NAVFAC Beaufort utility privatization reported at roughly $251.4 million over 50 years resolves in the federal award data to N69450-08-C-0070, awarded to the Beaufort-Jasper Water & Sewer Authority on 2008-02-28 with a period of performance to 2058-02-27 — exactly 50 years — and a current base-and-all-options value of $254,977,740.80, close to but not identical with the reported figure. The material correction is the commodity: the contract covers the water distribution and wastewater collection systems at MCRD Parris Island, MCAS Beaufort, the Naval Hospital and Laurel Bay housing. It contains no electricity. USAspending shows only $20,987,602.80 obligated, but the award record was last modified on 2019-07-16, so that obligation figure is a floor that stops eleven years into a fifty-year term rather than a current total.
cases.microreactor_read: A quarter-billion-dollar, fifty-year Beaufort utility deal is real but it is not an electricity market, so it prices nothing a reactor sells; the number to carry forward from Beaufort is the separate $212.7M Parris Island ESPC, not this one. The transferable fact is structural: DoD is comfortable handing a single counterparty a 50-year franchise over a commodity utility at a base, and that is precisely the tenor a microreactor needs and cannot get from a construction contract.

cases.name: Salisbury VA Medical Center campus generator installation (36C24626C0037)

parties.host: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Salisbury VAMC

cases.capacity: Campus-wide standby generation for a VA medical center; kW rating not stated in the award record
cases.capex: $23,905,280 obligated; base and all options identical, period of performance 2026-05-14 to 2027-07-28
cases.displaced: Nothing — this is new or replacement standby diesel capacity bought to keep a hospital campus alive through grid outages

filings.type: Definitive contract, PSC Y1DZ construction of other hospital buildings

cases.summary: VA Network Contracting Office 6 awarded Valiant Construction LLC $23,905,280 on 2026-05-14 to install a campus generator at the Salisbury VA Medical Center, with a period of performance to 2027-07-28 and no unexercised options. The award buys standby capacity only: the generators run during outages and testing, not as a source of energy. This is one of a class — the same sweep surfaced VA generator awards of $22.9M in New York, $19.0M in Maryland and $10.3M at Loma Linda in California — so $10M to $24M per hospital campus is the going federal rate for backup power that produces almost no kilowatt-hours.
cases.microreactor_read: A single VA hospital campus is willing to spend $23.9 million on diesel plant that will idle for 8,700 hours a year, and it will do it again in fifteen or twenty years. That is the number a 1-5 MW microreactor has to be measured against at a medical campus — not the hospital's energy bill, but its resilience capex, because the reactor is the only product that can be charged to both budget lines at once.

cases.name: San Juan VA Medical Center generator farm hurricane hardening (36C24826C0006)

parties.host: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, VA Caribbean Healthcare System

cases.capacity: Existing on-site generator farm serving a VA medical center; kW rating not stated in the award record
cases.capex: $10,835,000 obligated; base and all options identical, period of performance 2026-04-22 to 2028-09-05
cases.displaced: Nothing is displaced — the award hardens diesel plant that already exists so it survives the next hurricane

filings.type: Definitive contract, PSC Z2DA repair or alteration of hospitals and infirmaries

cases.summary: VA Network Contract Office 8 awarded Project Management Solutions LLC $10,835,000 on 2026-04-22 for construction to hurricane-harden the generator farm at the VA medical campus in San Juan, Puerto Rico, running to 2028-09-05. The scope is the enclosure and protection of existing diesel plant, not new capacity and not energy. On an island whose grid has failed repeatedly, the VA is spending eleven million dollars purely on making its backup diesels weatherproof — a cost line that exists only because the primary supply is untrustworthy and the backup is exposed.
cases.microreactor_read: Hurricane hardening is a recurring cost that a buried or hardened microreactor would not incur in the same form, and Puerto Rico prices it at $10.8M for one hospital's generator yard alone. Selling into a Caribbean medical campus means beating the sum of three lines the VA already pays separately — backup capex in the $10-24M band, hardening at $10.8M, and grid energy at PREPA's rates — rather than beating any one of them.
